No doubt we all long for a joy which no man can take
from us. But do we wish for it in all seriousness? If so,
then we must realize this: that we are aspiring to a joy
which does not cling to this world. We must become clear
about this noteworthy fact, namely that no one can tell us
what is the true object of such joy. No one can tell us at
what, on this level, we can and should rejoice. For every-
thing that might be named as its object would still belong to
this old world. And if for many centuries the pious have
dreamed of such joy in their fanciful pictures of the heavenly
city with its golden streets, and of the choirs and songs of the
new Jerusalem where the blessed live for evermore, we must
say that all such pictures are mere images and symbols for a
joy that is inexpressible. For the ineffable joy which no man
can take from us, no object can be named in human terms
and concepts.
Or may perhaps one ideal object of such joy be formu-
lated? Yes, there is one thing we can say: it is the joy of
freedom—of freedom from the world, the joy that the ques-
tions and cares of the world can no longer concern us
in our innermost being, because we no longer belong to the
world. It is the joy of a freedom that may perhaps be under-
stood if we reflect that once a message of understanding and
forgiving love freed us from a heavy inner burden which we
dragged around with us, a burden which lay oppressively on
our minds and spirits and which tainted with a touch of
bitterness even our happiest hours. What joyful relief it was
for us when a word of divine forgiveness effaced our past and
delivered us from its dead weight! We then rejoiced—-but at
what? At nothing in particular, at nothing specific, simply
over the fact that we were free. Or perhaps it has been our
experience that we were once entangled in an unendurable
situation, whether innocently or guiltily, and there came a
day which set us free, whether by our own decision or by a
favourable juncture of circumstances; the past sank away
